lesson.menu_title: I Regret to Say, I Regret Saying — When the Form Changes the Meaning
lesson.menu_desc: A correspondent’s memoir and the verbs that mean one thing with -ing and another with to -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- I Regret to Say, I Regret Saying
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Henrique Monteiro Neto | Lesson 16 -- I Regret to Say, I Regret Saying

listenings.text: People ask me whether I kept a diary in those years, and the honest answer is that I tried to keep one and gave up after a month. What I have instead are notebooks, and the notebooks are humbling. I remember writing certain sentences, word for word, and when I go back to the page, the sentence is not there. Something else is there, flatter and more careful. So I stopped trusting my memory of the notebooks and started trusting the notebooks themselves, which is harder than it sounds, because the notebooks are less flattering. The memory has had thirty years to improve the story. The page has not. If there is a rule I follow in the book, it is this one: where the two disagree, the page wins, and I say so in the text.

I read memoirs for a living, and I would ask you to read them the way a historian does, which is gratefully and suspiciously at the same time. Gratefully, because a memoir records what nobody else was in a position to see: the mood in a room, the hour at which a decision was really made. Suspiciously, because every memoir is written by the one person with the strongest interest in how the story ends. Notice which mistakes the author owns up to. They are almost always the small, forgivable ones. The large ones tend to be described in the passive voice, or not at all. And when a writer says they regret not having said something at the time, ask yourself why they are saying it now, and to whom.

extra_audio.text: Clara says she remembers filing the story that night, but the notebook shows she filed it two days later. Henrique asks whether she regrets writing the book at all. She says she regrets not checking her own notes sooner, and that she went on to rewrite three chapters. He asks why she did not simply stop to correct the dates. She explains that the mistake itself was worth keeping, because it shows how memory improves a story.

reading.rtitle: The Night I Did Not File
paras: I remember standing on the hotel roof that night, watching the tanks come down the avenue, and I remember thinking that I would never see anything like it again. I was wrong about that, as it turned out, but I was right to stop and look. Most of my colleagues had gone back inside to file. I stayed, and I have never regretted staying.

What I do regret is what I wrote the following morning. I had tried to reach three sources overnight and had reached none of them, so I tried quoting a fourth, a man I had met only once, and his account went out under my name. I forgot to mention that he had a brother in the government. I have not forgotten it since.

My editor called at noon. I regret to say that I defended the piece for a full ten minutes before she stopped me. She did not stop to argue; she simply read the quotation back to me, slowly, and asked what I would have made of it if somebody else had written it. I meant to answer her. I could not.

I went on to cover that country for eleven more years, and I went on writing about that night for most of them, as though the next version might finally be the accurate one. It took me a long time to accept that the story I remember telling is not the story I told. The archive has the second one. This book is an attempt to stop improving it.
